## Company: LT Group, Inc. (LTG)
Sector: Holding Firms / Holding Firms
LT Group, Inc. (LTG), formerly Tanduay Holdings, Inc. (THI), was incorporated on May 25, 1937 under the name The Manila Wine Merchants, Inc. to engage in the trading business. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the change in corporate name to Asian Pacific Equity Corporation on September 22, 1995 and the change of its primary purpose to that of a holding company. On November 10, 1999, the corporate name was again changed to THI. On September 28, 2012, the SEC approved the change in the corporate name to the present one.

After a series of restructuring activities in 2012 and 2013, LTG expanded and diversified its investments to include the beverages; tobacco; property development; and banking businesses. The Company's subsidiaries and associates are Tanduay Distillers, Inc.; Asia Brewery, Incorporated; Fortune Tobacco Corporation; Philippine National Bank; Saturn Holdings, Inc.; Paramount Landequities, Inc.; and Eton Properties Philippines, Inc.

thesis:
LT Group, Inc. is a conglomerate most Filipinos interact with daily without knowing it — Fortune Tobacco's cigarette brands dominate the local market, Asia Brewery produces affordable beer and non-alcoholic beverages, Tanduay rum is the world's best-selling rum by volume, and Philippine National Bank is one of the country's top universal banks. Add property and retail assets and the picture is complete: this is a business easy to understand, anchored in consumer staples and financial services, operating in a market of 115 million people with rising incomes.

The moat is real but narrow and sector-specific. Fortune Tobacco benefits from massive distribution scale, brand loyalty in the mass market, and the structural protection of illicit-trade crackdowns that favor compliant incumbents. PNB carries a strong franchise in OFW remittances and SME lending, segments with genuine switching costs. Asia Brewery competes head-to-head with San Miguel in beer — a tougher position — but benefits from LTG's shared distribution muscle. The tobacco business faces a secular volume decline globally, but in the Philippines, volume has held surprisingly well, and the mandatory 5% annual excise escalator under RA 11346 actually acts as a predictable pricing mechanism that incumbents can pass through. The risk is long-dated regulatory tightening (plain packaging, smoking bans) accelerating the secular decline faster than earnings from PNB and liquor can compensate.

Management under Lucio Tan III is the clearest red flag and the clearest buy signal at the same time. The Tan family controls the conglomerate and has a well-documented history of value leakage through related-party transactions and conglomerate discount. That said, record H1 2026 profit of ₱17B — 14% above prior year — with PNB contributing ₱8.2B and Fortune Tobacco ₱6.1B, demonstrates operational execution that is hard to argue with. Regular dividend declarations (8.3% yield at current price) show willingness to return cash; dividends are not a window dressing item at this payout level. There are no recent disclosures suggesting governance deterioration, and government enforcement against illicit cigarette imports actually validates management's legitimate-trade positioning.

Valuation is where the thesis gets complicated. At ₱15.04, LTG trades at 5.3x earnings, 0.7x book, and an 8.3% yield — numbers that scream "cheap." The Rule #1 Sticker Price of ₱16.20 implies the stock is trading near fair value by that framework, which means no margin of safety by Phil Town's standards. The 50% MOS buy price of $8.10 is 46% below current price — a level the stock has not seen recently and would require a material earnings deterioration or broader market selloff to reach. The 10-year average ROIC of 11.2% and EPS growth of 16.7% are respectable for a conglomerate, but the conglomerate structure inherently makes it difficult to assess the quality of each segment's ROIC independently. FCF growth of 81.7% (10-year average) is distorted by base effects; free cash flow from banking subsidiaries is not comparable to industrial FCF.

The bottom line is a **watch**. LTG is a genuinely understandable, moat-adjacent business with real earnings momentum and a generous dividend, but at ₱15.04, it sits 85% above the margin-of-safety entry price. Phil Town's framework demands waiting for a proper discount to intrinsic value, and that discipline is correct here: tobacco has a long shadow of regulatory risk, the conglomerate structure obscures capital allocation quality, and family control creates persistent discount. Watch for the stock to pull back toward ₱10–12 on any market correction or earnings disappointment, which would compress the MOS gap meaningfully. A secondary trigger to upgrade to buy would be any sign that PNB's OFW franchise is compounding faster than expected, or that Fortune Tobacco's volumes stabilize rather than declining — either of which would justify a higher Sticker Price.
